About

I think about self-love as a relational attitude and about its ethical role in agency, emotional autonomy, friendship, and solidarity. Kant has been my primary interlocutor here, along with Aristotle and Rousseau. Although the Kantian framework is my home turf for investigating moral matters, my questions about self-love are inspired by diverse intellectual sensibilities, from Audre Lorde, María Lugones, Simone de Beauvoir, and Hannah Arendt to Henri Nouwen and, more recently, Iris Murdoch.

My background is in moral and political theory and their history, with a focus on Kant’s practical philosophy. I also have evolving interests at the intersection of aesthetics and ethics, and in bringing Kantian approaches to cultivating moral feeling into conversation with Mengzi’s account of compassion.

I’m currently a philosophy postdoctoral faculty fellow at Northwestern University’s Brady Program for Ethics & Civic Life. I received my PhD from the University of California, Riverside, where I also taught classes in philosophy of feminism, social and political philosophy, and the early modern tradition.

Teaching

My primary aim in teaching is to foster intellectual autonomy through serious play. Philosophical growth demands a willingness to take intellectual risks. But this requires a secure environment in which we venture into uncertain terrain together. To cultivate skills for meaningful engagement in this joint enterprise, my course design strives to provide students with creative ways to 1) collectively practice philosophical skills in reading, writing, and critical thinking and 2) promote inclusive, student-centered learning.

Dissertation

A Kantian Duty of Moral Self-Love
(Spring 2025)

Moral practice often invokes self-love, and imperatives to “radical self-love” in social justice discourse have become an urgent call to solidarity and resistance for oppressed groups to have “pride” in their marginalized identities. Yet, self-love remains largely neglected in the philosophical literature on moral self-regard. The moral tradition tends to treat self-love as an inevitable feature of human psychology that we must curb for the sake of others. Indeed, Kant infamously regards self-love as morality’s chief antagonist. However, I propose that a moral conception of proper self-love can be grown on Kantian soil. This dissertation articulates a Kantian moral theoretical basis for proper self-love and argues that as members of the moral community, we have a duty of self-love because this kind of self-regard is central to our moral relations, and thus moral agency. As an alternative to Kant’s more famous notion of self-interested self-love, moral self-love positively values oneself as an end-in-itself. As practical, moral self-love is a form of self-regard that transforms how we relate to the value of our ends and enables us to sustain the kind of joint willing that constitutes our participation in sustaining the integrity of our moral relations.

Book Project

Self-Love & Solidarity

What started as a concern that care be taken as seriously as autonomy in our moral regard for others has led to a complicated conception of love as a free power of connection. (If anyone has a better idea for what to call this, I am desperate to hear from you!) It is at once a universal language of connection, but one that understands itself as aiming at contact with a distinct subjectivity. Its normativity, I suspect, has something to do with loving a subject under the idea of freedom. This project is an attempt to address certain dualisms that my dissertation began to deconstruct from a Kantian framework—between the universal and particular, duty and care, the personal and the distal, respect and love, and—my most enduring bugbear—reason and sensibility.

Monograph proposal. Nominated for the Kaplan Institute for the Humanities Dissertation to Book Workshop, Northwestern University, March 2025.
